body.back: Latin for strangling of the chest: chest pain from reduced blood flow to the heart (myocardial ischaemia). Transient ischaemia without infarction, unlike a heart attack, which causes permanent damage.
Squeezing pain or heaviness in the chest, spreading to neck, jaw, arms, shoulders or back, with dyspnoea and sweating. In the elderly: stomach-area pain after meals. In women: burning or tenderness.

The most common form: coronary atherosclerosis over 70 percent cannot meet demand on exercise or stress; relieved by rest. Subendocardial ischaemia releases adenosine and bradykinin. ECG: ST depression. Other causes: hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, aortic stenosis, hypertension (thick muscle needing more oxygen).

A clot forms on the plaque, leaving even less room for flow: pain on exertion or at rest that does not go away. Tissue is alive but ischaemic: an emergency with high infarction risk. ECG: ST depression.

Vasospastic angina from coronary artery spasm, with or without atherosclerosis, possibly involving thromboxane A2. Occurs at rest, often at night, triggered by stress, smoking or cocaine; often severe. Transmural ischaemia gives ST elevation. Diagnosed by provocation with ergonovine or acetylcholine; responds to medication.

title: Compare the three types of angina.
subject: subj:semio

body.front: Compare the three types of angina.
body.back: All reversible, without permanent injury. Stable: exertional, relieved by rest, ST depression. Unstable: at rest too, persistent, ST depression, emergency. Prinzmetal: any time including rest, ST elevation (transmural), treated with nitroglycerin and calcium channel blockers.
ECG during attacks (ST depression or elevation), stress test, and imaging such as coronary angiography. Microvascular angina (cardiac syndrome X) involves small vessels.

Lifestyle: stop smoking, limit alcohol, healthy weight and diet, regular but not excessive exercise, avoid stress and large meals. Drugs: sublingual nitroglycerin, long-acting nitrates, aspirin, beta blockers, calcium channel blockers. Surgery: angioplasty, bypass.

title: Define arrhythmia and give AFib numbers.
subject: subj:semio

body.front: Define arrhythmia and give AFib numbers.
body.back: An irregular heart rhythm. Atrial fibrillation is the most common significant arrhythmia: 33.5 million in 2010, almost 59 million in 2019, projected to rise over 60 percent by 2050.

Cardiac: chest pain, tachycardia, irregular heartbeat, flutters, leg swelling (right heart failure). General: fatigue even after rest, stress, dizziness or faintness, confusion. Some patients have no symptoms.

Depolarisation starts in the SA node pacemaker cells, spreads through the atria, passes the AV node, then the bundle of His and Purkinje fibres through the ventricles. This orderly sequence produces the ECG.

The ECG plots voltage against time. P wave: atrial depolarisation, right atrium slightly before left. QRS: near-simultaneous ventricular depolarisation, 0.08 to 0.12 s; longer is wide. T wave: ventricular repolarisation.
The sinus node is inhibited; migrating wavelets of re-entrant activation replace coordinated atrial activity, sending irregular impulses to the AV node.
Structural heart disease: hypertension (atrial enlargement and fibrosis), coronary artery disease (ischaemia, scarring), valvular disease (especially mitral), heart failure and cardiomyopathy.
Blood stagnates in the left atrial appendage (Virchow's triad), clots form and embolise to the cerebral arteries. Stroke risk rises about five-fold; stroke can also cause AFib.

Flutter: organised re-entrant circuit, atrial rate 250 to 350, often regular ventricular response, sawtooth F waves, milder symptoms, increased stroke risk. AFib: chaotic, 350 to 600, irregularly irregular, no P waves, high stroke risk. Prevalence about 9 to 1, both rising with age.
The ABC pathway: stroke prevention (anticoagulation), rhythm control, cardiac ablation, and left atrial appendage occlusion when treatment fails.
Heart rate, respiratory rate and blood pressure are needed for every patient and are a basic physician skill.

title: How are vital signs taken correctly?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: How are vital signs taken correctly?
body.back: Patient resting comfortably, supine in hospital or sitting elsewhere, for 3 to 5 minutes, no blood draw before; explain what you do; use a bare arm; avoid an arm with a problem or on the mastectomy side.

title: What do you inspect on the thorax?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: What do you inspect on the thorax?
body.back: Scars (a vertical sternal scar means prior open-heart surgery) and deformities: pectus excavatum and carinatum, which with ligamentous hypermobility may suggest Marfan syndrome. Also look at eyes, limbs and neck veins.

title: Name eye signs of cardiovascular disease.
subject: subj:semio

body.front: Name eye signs of cardiovascular disease.
body.back: Xanthelasma: yellow eyelid plaques suggesting hypercholesterolaemia. Roth spots: retinal red rings with white centres, classic of infective endocarditis but seen in only about 2 percent.

title: What do clubbing and cyanosis mean?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: What do clubbing and cyanosis mean?
body.back: Clubbing: flat, broad fingertips, from lung disease or chronic hypoxaemia, occasionally normal. Cyanosis implies poor perfusion; central is more serious than peripheral. At Hb 10 g/dL it appears only near 70 percent saturation, so cyanosis in severe anaemia means critical illness.

title: Name the endocarditis lesions of the hands and feet.
subject: subj:semio

body.front: Name the endocarditis lesions of the hands and feet.
body.back: Osler nodes: raised, painful, red (immune complexes). Janeway lesions: small, red, painless. Splinter haemorrhages: short dark lines under the nails (microemboli).

Observe the right IJV with the patient supine, head raised 15 to 45 degrees and turned left. Press the right upper quadrant for a few seconds; measure the top of the column above the sternal angle. Positive: a sustained rise over 4 cm. It reflects right heart function and CVP, not dehydration.

Congestion of peripheral tissues: distended jugular veins, dependent oedema of legs, ankles and arms, ascites, enlarged liver and spleen, anorexia and GI distress, fatigue. It may be secondary to chronic lung disease (cor pulmonale).
The heart muscle does not pump blood as well as it should; blood backs up and fluid can build up in the lungs (pulmonary oedema), causing breathlessness.

Systolic: cannot pump hard enough; stretched, thin chambers; ejection fraction 40 percent or less. Diastolic: cannot fill enough; stiff, thick chambers; ejection fraction normal but stroke volume still low.

title: Why does heart failure cause arrhythmias?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: Why does heart failure cause arrhythmias?
body.back: Stretched thin walls or thick ischaemic walls irritate the heart cells, triggering arrhythmias.

title: List the symptoms of heart failure.
subject: subj:semio

body.front: List the symptoms of heart failure.
body.back: Shortness of breath, chest pain on exertion, dizziness, swelling of legs, hands and feet, sudden weight gain, fatigue and weakness.

Stroke volume = EDV minus ESV (135 minus 65 = 70 mL). Cardiac output = HR x SV (70 x 70 = about 5 L/min). Ejection fraction normal about 64 to 70 percent; borderline 40 to 50; systolic failure 40 or below.
More ventricular filling (preload) stretches the fibres like a rubber band and increases stroke volume. Sympathetic activation adds to it by emptying the ventricle more fully.

title: List the causes of heart failure.
subject: subj:semio

body.front: List the causes of heart failure.
body.back: Heart attack and coronary disease, valve conditions, obesity, arrhythmia, high blood pressure, diabetes, cardiomyopathy and myocarditis.

title: How does hypertension cause left heart failure?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: How does hypertension cause left heart failure?
body.back: Higher arterial pressure makes pumping harder, the ventricle hypertrophies, squeezes its coronaries and needs more oxygen, and contractions weaken: usually systolic failure. Long-standing hypertension also causes diastolic failure.

title: How do the kidneys respond in heart failure?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: How do the kidneys respond in heart failure?
body.back: Reduced renal flow activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, retaining fluid; filling, preload and contraction strength rise, at the cost of congestion.

title: Name causes of diastolic left heart failure.
subject: subj:semio

body.front: Name causes of diastolic left heart failure.
body.back: Long-standing hypertension, aortic stenosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and restrictive cardiomyopathy.

title: Describe pulmonary oedema in left heart failure.
subject: subj:semio

body.front: Describe pulmonary oedema in left heart failure.
body.back: Raised pulmonary venous pressure makes vessels leak: dyspnoea, orthopnoea, crackles, bloody froth, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea (waking 1 to 2 hours after sleep, drowning sensation), trouble speaking in full sentences, anxiety, reduced alertness, pallor and sweating.
Q = ΔP / R: flow equals pressure difference over resistance; raising resistance at constant pressure lowers flow.
Left coronary flow is highest in diastole, when the myocardium relaxes and stops compressing its vessels.

The healthy endothelium releases nitric oxide, relaxing smooth muscle. Risk factors cause impaired NO production, oxidative stress, inflammation, leucocyte adhesion, vasoconstriction (endothelin-1, angiotensin II, thromboxane A2), and lead to atherosclerosis initiation, progression, plaque rupture and atherothrombosis.

title: Link coronary disease to angina and infarction.
subject: subj:semio

body.front: Link coronary disease to angina and infarction.
body.back: Normal artery, atherosclerosis, atherosclerosis with clot, or coronary spasm. Angina: transient ischaemia without infarction. Heart attack: permanent damage.

title: Give the global burden of cardiovascular disease.
subject: subj:semio

body.front: Give the global burden of cardiovascular disease.
body.back: The leading cause of death worldwide, about 17.7 million deaths a year, though in high-income countries cancer causes twice as many deaths.

Over 70 percent is due to modifiable risk factors: metabolic (hypertension, diabetes, cholesterol, waist-to-hip ratio), behavioural (tobacco, alcohol, poor diet, low activity), environmental (household air pollution), psychosocial (depression, low education) and low strength. Their weight differs by country income, so strategies must be local.

title: Revise heart failure in one card.
subject: subj:semio

body.front: Revise heart failure in one card.
body.back: Systolic: can't pump, thin chambers. Diastolic: can't fill, thick chambers. Left: pulmonary oedema, orthopnoea, PND, crackles. Right: jugular distension, hepatosplenomegaly, ascites, pitting oedema (legs standing, sacrum lying).

Stable: plaque, exertion, relieved by rest, ST depression. Unstable: clot on plaque, rest pain, emergency, ST depression. Prinzmetal: spasm, any time, ST elevation; nitroglycerin and calcium channel blockers.
Most often left heart failure (biventricular). Also left-to-right shunts through atrial or ventricular septal defects, and chronic lung disease such as COPD (cor pulmonale).

title: How does left heart failure lead to right heart failure?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: How does left heart failure lead to right heart failure?
body.back: Backed-up blood raises pulmonary artery pressure, making it harder for the right ventricle to pump; it eventually fails.

title: How do septal defects cause right heart failure?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: How do septal defects cause right heart failure?
body.back: Blood shunts from the high-pressure left side to the low-pressure right side, increasing right-sided volume, causing hypertrophy, ischaemia and systolic and diastolic dysfunction.

Chronic lung disease (chronic bronchitis, emphysema) causes hypoxia, which constricts pulmonary arterioles; pulmonary pressure rises and the right ventricle hypertrophies and fails. Chronic hypoxia also brings polycythaemia, systemic inflammation and endothelial dysfunction.
Mild: restlessness, headache, confusion, anxiety, dyspnoea. Severe: tachycardia, tachypnoea, bradycardia, extreme restlessness and cyanosis.

Jugular venous distension; backed-up liver and spleen, painful hepatosplenomegaly that can progress to cardiac cirrhosis and liver failure; ascites; pitting oedema of legs when standing and of the sacrum when lying.
Grade 1: 2 mm. Grade 2: 3 to 4 mm. Grade 3: 5 to 6 mm. Grade 4: 8 mm.
Fatigue, raised peripheral venous pressure, ascites, enlarged liver and spleen, distended jugular veins, anorexia and GI distress, weight gain, dependent oedema.

Left: decreased output and pulmonary congestion: activity intolerance, poor perfusion, cyanosis, orthopnoea, cough with frothy sputum, PND. Right: peripheral congestion: oedema, ascites, liver congestion and impaired liver function, GI congestion with anorexia and weight loss.
Cushing's syndrome is cortisol excess of any cause. Cushing's disease is specifically a pituitary ACTH-secreting source.

title: List the clinical signs of hypercortisolism.
subject: subj:semio

body.front: List the clinical signs of hypercortisolism.
body.back: Weight excess with truncal obesity, moon face and particular fat deposits; purple striae; hypertension; diabetes or prediabetes; acne; limb muscle atrophy; depression with suicide risk, or euphoria and delirium; thrombosis risk; osteoporosis; hirsutism and menstrual troubles in women; erectile dysfunction in men.
By ACTH: ACTH-dependent (high ACTH) from a pituitary or ectopic source; ACTH-independent (low ACTH) from an adrenal source.

Adrenal CT: gland structure and size, tumour cause, adenoma size and lipid content, tumour extension. MIBG scintigraphy: functional evaluation of catecholamine-secreting tissue, unilateral secretion (adenoma or hyperplasia) or ectopic secretion; paragangliomas are possible along the sympathetic chain.
Chronic hyperglycaemia due to an absolute or relative deficiency of insulin secretion and/or insulin action (insulin resistance).
Fasting under 1.10 g/L; under 1.40 g/L 2 hours after an OGTT.
By chance; from hyperglycaemia symptoms; at an acute or chronic complication. Average delay 2 to 3 years after onset.

title: The hyperglycaemia syndrome and its mechanisms?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: The hyperglycaemia syndrome and its mechanisms?
body.back: Polyuria (glycosuria, osmotic diuresis), polydipsia (from the polyuria), weight loss (no insulin, so lipolysis), compensatory polyphagia.

title: Other symptoms that can reveal diabetes?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: Other symptoms that can reveal diabetes?
body.back: Blurred vision, fatigue, slow-healing cuts, nausea or abdominal pain, paresthesia, nocturia. Ketosis: acetone breath, Kussmaul breathing.
About 1.8 g/L: above it, glucose appears in the urine (urine strip).
Fasting ≥ 1.26 g/L on 2 samples; 2-hour OGTT ≥ 2 g/L; HbA1c ≥ 6.5%; random ≥ 2 g/L with classic symptoms.
HbA1c 5.7 to 6.4%; fasting 1.00 to 1.25 g/L; 2-hour OGTT 1.40 to 1.99 g/L.
Under 40, acute onset, thin or normal, marked symptoms, ketosis or ketoacidosis at onset, autoimmune, no cardiovascular risk factors, insulin for life. 10 to 15%.

Over 40, family history, overweight, progressive onset, few symptoms, sometimes found at a complication, no inaugural ketoacidosis, cardiovascular risk factors. 85 to 90%. Check complications at diagnosis.
Sella turcica below, optic chiasm above, cavernous sinuses on both sides (with cranial nerves III, IV and VI). Size about 5 × 10 × 15 mm.

title: Hyperprolactinaemia: signs in women and in men?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: Hyperprolactinaemia: signs in women and in men?
body.back: Women: galactorrhoea, amenorrhoea or oligomenorrhoea, infertility, low libido. Men: hypogonadism, low libido first, erectile dysfunction, gynaecomastia, infertility. Mass effect only with macroadenomas.
Prolactin assay with PEG precipitation (to exclude macroprolactin), then pituitary MRI: micro- or macro/invasive prolactinoma.

Physiological: pregnancy, nursing, nipple stimulation, exercise, stress, sleep, seizures. Drugs: dopamine antagonists (phenothiazines, haloperidol, risperidone, metoclopramide), opioids, verapamil, methyldopa. Disease: pituitary tumours, hypothyroidism, chronic kidney disease, liver failure, stalk lesion.
Frontal bossing and prominent supraorbital ridges, big nose, prognathism, teeth separation and malocclusion, coarse features, deep nasolabial furrows, macroglossia, thick lips, deep voice.

Big thick hands and feet; oily sweaty skin; visceromegaly; arthropathy; carpal tunnel in up to half; sleep apnoea; colonic polyps; hypertension and LVH; diabetes, hypertriglyceridaemia, hypercalciuria, goitre.
High IGF-1 and GH not suppressed during a 75 g OGTT (above 0.4 µg/L). Measure prolactin too (co-secretion). Then pituitary MRI.

title: Visual signs of pituitary mass effect?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: Visual signs of pituitary mass effect?
body.back: Chiasm: bitemporal loss from the superior fields (quadrantanopia, then hemianopia). Cavernous sinus: III, IV, VI palsy, so diplopia and ptosis. Rarely lower acuity, optic atrophy, papilloedema.
Bleeding into a pituitary tumour. Emergency: sudden severe headache, visual loss, ophthalmoplegia, meningism, altered consciousness. Often leaves hypopituitarism. Early transsphenoidal decompression.
Pallor, loss of body hair (axillary and pubic), depigmentation (areolas, genitals). Thin, cold, dry skin. (Not on this midterm.)

Inspection: swelling (the normal thyroid is not visible), inflammation, dilated cervical veins. Palpation of the gland. Auscultation: a bruit indicates high blood flow in hyperthyroidism, sometimes with a thrill.

TSH, free T4 and free T3. Ultrasound describes size, structure, volume, nodules (size, solid or liquid, margins, vascularity, micro- or macrocalcifications) and lymph nodes. Scintigraphy shows uptake.

title: How are goitre and nodules evaluated?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: How are goitre and nodules evaluated?
body.back: Normal thyroid: height 4 to 6 cm, width and thickness 1.5 to 2.5 cm; goitre if thickness over 2.5 cm or volume over 18 cm³ (women) or 20 cm³ (men). 90 to 95 percent of lumps are benign. Red flags: hoarseness, nodes, stridor. Ultrasound U1 to U5; FNAC for U3 to U5. Cancer work-up: palpation, ultrasound, hormones and calcitonin, FNA, histology.

General: fatigue, weight loss despite increased appetite. Cardiovascular: resting tachycardia, palpitations, exertional dyspnoea, loud heart sounds, systolic murmur, raised systolic BP. Hot sweaty skin, heat intolerance. Fine tremor, hyperkinesia, hyperreflexia, amyotrophy, weakness. Soft stools. Emotional lability, irritability, insomnia. Eyes: lid retraction, lid lag, rare blinking, eyelid tremor.

The commonest cause of hyperthyroidism: autoimmune, genetically predisposed, mostly women aged 20 to 40, relapsing and remitting. TSH receptor antibodies are highly specific; ultrasound shows enlarged volume with increased vascularity; scintigraphy shows diffuse homogeneous uptake. Diagnosis: thyrotoxicosis + goitre + exophthalmos.

Inflammation of orbital muscles, periocular tissue and retro-orbital fat: lid retraction, exophthalmos, chemosis, scleral injection, diplopia, muscle dysfunction, and reduced acuity from optic neuropathy.

title: Toxic adenoma versus toxic multinodular goitre.
subject: subj:semio

body.front: Toxic adenoma versus toxic multinodular goitre.
body.back: Toxic adenoma: a single hypersecreting nodule, thyrotoxicosis without eye signs, a hot nodule on scintigraphy with suppressed contralateral lobe. Toxic multinodular goitre: older patients with long-standing goitre becoming toxic; look for compression; multiple hot nodules or patchy uptake.

Hyperthyroidism: Graves', toxic nodular goitre, toxic adenoma, Jod-Basedow, metastatic follicular cancer, trophoblastic tumours. Thyrotoxicosis without hyperthyroidism: subacute and silent thyroiditis, ectopic thyroid, struma ovarii. Thyroiditis releases stored hormone transiently.

Deficient thyroid hormone slowing metabolism; primary or secondary (pituitary). Causes: iatrogenic (thyroidectomy, radioiodine, irradiation, drugs such as lithium and amiodarone), thyroiditis (Hashimoto's, de Quervain, postpartum, Riedel), iodine deficiency, congenital, central.

Hypometabolism: physical, psychological, intellectual and sexual asthenia. TSH markedly raised, FT4 and FT3 low. Organ effects: macrocytic anaemia, dilutional hyponatraemia, hypercholesterolaemia, hyperprolactinaemia. Anti-TPO and anti-Tg antibodies for aetiology.

Myxoedema coma: rare end stage in the elderly, with stupor, hypothermia, hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, hypoventilation, shock and death. Cardiovascular: myxoedema cardiomyopathy and heart failure, pericardial effusion, coronary disease from high cholesterol.

title: Name the forms of GI bleeding.
subject: subj:semio

body.front: Name the forms of GI bleeding.
body.back: Haematemesis (vomited blood, upper tract), melena (black tarry digested stools, 6 to 8 h after onset, mostly upper), haematochezia (bright red rectal blood, lower tract or massive upper), occult bleeding (anaemia or positive FOBT).

title: What are the three levels of diagnosis?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: What are the three levels of diagnosis?
body.back: Positive (is the bleeding digestive?), topographic (upper or lower?), etiological (what lesion?).

title: What are the differentials of haematemesis and melena?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: What are the differentials of haematemesis and melena?
body.back: Haematemesis: hemoptysis (frothy, with cough), swallowed epistaxis, gum bleeding, coloured food or drugs. Melena: iron, charcoal, bismuth, some foods.

Warning: pallor, cold extremities, restlessness, tachycardia. Severe: hypotension, polypnoea, oliguria, altered consciousness, mottling. Haemoglobin falls, but a normal value does not rule out recent bleeding. Haematemesis with melena or rectal bleeding means abundant bleeding.

ICU or emergency admission; two large-bore IV lines; CBC, group, crossmatch, ionogram, creatinine, liver tests; crystalloids and transfusion; oxygen; gastric tube and urinary catheter; continuous monitoring of BP, pulse, urine output, consciousness.

Upper: peptic ulcer, oesophageal or gastric varices, Mallory-Weiss tear, erosive gastritis, cancer, stress ulcers, NSAIDs and aspirin. Lower: haemorrhoids, fissure, fistula, anal cancer; colorectal cancer or polyps, diverticular disease, angiodysplasia, IBD; small bowel malformations, tumours, Meckel's diverticulum.

Resuscitation, oxygen, transfusion, PPIs if peptic. Endoscopic haemostasis: injection (adrenaline, sclerosant), thermal coagulation, clips, variceal band ligation. Surgery for refractory bleeding or perforation. Prognosis is worse with varices and cancer.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Endoscopy. Upper endoscopy finds the source in over 90%; colonoscopy for lower bleeding; treats by injection, coagulation, clips, banding.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Haematemesis. Vomiting red or black blood; lesion above the angle of Treitz.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Haematochezia. Bright red blood per anus; usually lower GI, or massive upper bleeding.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Melaena. Black, tarry, smelly stools of digested blood; usually upper GI; appears 6-8 h after bleeding starts.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Occult bleeding. Revealed only by anaemia or a positive faecal occult blood test.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Emergency measures. ICU, two large-bore IV lines, bloods and cross-match, fluids, oxygen, monitoring.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Severity. Pallor, cold extremities, tachycardia; then hypotension, oliguria, confusion, mottling.
Haematemesis (vomiting blood), melaena (black tarry stools), haematochezia (bright red rectal blood), occult (anaemia or positive FOBT).
Positive (is it digestive?), topographic (upper or lower?), etiological (which lesion?).
Haematemesis: haemoptysis, swallowed epistaxis, gum bleeding, coloured food. Melaena: iron, charcoal, bismuth, foods.

title: Signs of severity in GI bleeding?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: Signs of severity in GI bleeding?
body.back: Warning: pallor, cold extremities, restlessness, tachycardia. Severe: hypotension, polypnoea, oliguria, altered consciousness, mottling.
ICU/emergency admission, two large-bore IV lines, CBC, group and cross-match, ionogram, creatinine, liver tests, fluids/transfusion, oxygen, gastric tube, urinary catheter, monitoring.
Peptic ulcer, varices, Mallory-Weiss tear, erosive gastritis/duodenitis, cancer, stress ulcers, NSAIDs/aspirin.
Anal (haemorrhoids, fissure, fistula, cancer), colorectal (cancer, polyps, diverticula, angiodysplasia, IBD), small bowel (malformations, tumours, Meckel's).
Injection (adrenaline, sclerosant), thermal coagulation, haemoclips, variceal band ligation; surgery if refractory or perforated.
Three angles: clinical, fewer than 3 stools a week; quantitative, under 100 g/day; qualitative, hard dehydrated stools. One of the commonest GI complaints.
Primary (functional): often chronic and isolated, by slow transit or outlet dysfunction. Secondary: more recent, a symptom of an underlying digestive or non-digestive condition.

title: Explain slow transit and outlet dysfunction.
subject: subj:semio

body.front: Explain slow transit and outlet dysfunction.
body.back: Slow transit: delayed movement through the colon, from reduced motility or spasticity, enteric nerve disorders. Outlet dysfunction: poor rectal propulsion or high resistance, e.g. the pelvic floor failing to relax, causing incomplete evacuation.
Stool dehydration from slow transit; neurogenic and myogenic hypomotility; hormonal and metabolic factors such as thyroid hormones and cortisol.

Chronic digestive disease, diabetes, neurological disorders; risk factors (age, low-fibre diet, sedentary life, pregnancy); surgery; medications (opioids, iron); family history of colorectal cancer. Characteristics: duration, frequency, straining, stool form, incomplete evacuation, blockage sensation, manual manoeuvres, laxatives.

Weight and nutrition. Abdomen: distension, tenderness, masses; absent sounds (ileus) or hyperactive (obstruction); tympany or faecal dullness. Rectal: squatting and straining for prolapse, knee-chest or left lateral; inspect for haemorrhoids, fissures, fistulas; feel impaction, tone and masses. Pelvic and neurological exams as needed.

title: When and how is constipation investigated?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: When and how is constipation investigated?
body.back: Indications: persistent constipation, failed treatment, need to type it, red flags (bleeding, weight loss, anaemia, severe pain, family history). Organic work-up: colonoscopy, CT or MRI, blood count, thyroid, electrolytes (calcium, potassium), glucose, coeliac serology. Functional: colonic transit study, defecography, anorectal manometry.

Secondary: colorectal tumours, strictures, megacolon, compression, fissures, prolapse, haemorrhoids; Parkinson's, MS, spinal cord injury, stroke; hypothyroidism, diabetes, hypercalcaemia, hypokalaemia, CKD; opioids, antidepressants, antihistamines, iron. Primary: slow transit (colonic inertia, spastic colon) or outlet (anismus, megarectum, rectocele, internal prolapse). IBS-C: pain, bloating, no organic cause.

Loose or watery stools with more frequency or volume: over 300 g/day, over 3 a day, water over 90 percent. Acute under 2 weeks (infection, food poisoning), prolonged 2 to 4 (post-infectious, parasitic), chronic over 4 (IBD, celiac, pancreatic insufficiency).
False diarrhoea (small hard stools, under 300 g/day), anal incontinence, and non-faecal discharge of blood, pus or mucus.

Secretory (choleriform): enterotoxin, profuse watery, dehydration, persists fasting (cholera, ETEC). Invasive (dysenteric): mucosal invasion, bloody mucus, fever, pain, tenesmus (Shigella, Salmonella, Campylobacter).

title: How do you assess acute diarrhoea?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: How do you assess acute diarrhoea?
body.back: Severity: extreme ages, immunosuppression, comorbidities; dehydration (dry tongue, thirst, skin folds, hypotension, oliguria); complications (colitis, sepsis). Cause: meals, collective exposure, travel, antibiotics, HIV or chemo; stool pattern. Tests only if severe, bloody, febrile, over 3 days, epidemic or immunosuppressed.

title: How do you assess chronic diarrhoea?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: How do you assess chronic diarrhoea?
body.back: History (onset, meals, stool aspect, weight loss, drugs, family history); exam with mandatory rectal exam and extra-abdominal signs. First-line bloods; second-line TSH, HIV, anti-transglutaminase, parasitology; EGD with duodenal biopsies and colonoscopy with biopsies; imaging.

title: Compare the mechanisms of chronic diarrhoea.
subject: subj:semio

body.front: Compare the mechanisms of chronic diarrhoea.
body.back: Osmotic: moderate, watery, stops fasting (lactose intolerance). Secretory: profuse, watery, persists (cholera, VIPoma, IBD, drugs). Malabsorptive: abundant, greasy, persists (celiac, pancreatic insufficiency). Motor: variable, food debris, stops fasting (IBS, hyperthyroidism). Exudative: protein loss (alpha-1 antitrypsin clearance).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Acute diarrhoea. Under 2 weeks; choleriform (secretory) or dysenteric (invasive).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Chronic diarrhoea. Over 4 weeks; identify the mechanism.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Definition. Stools over 300 g/day, more than 3 per day, over 90% water.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Malabsorptive diarrhoea. Abundant, greasy, pale, foul stools with deficiencies (coeliac, pancreatic insufficiency).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Motor diarrhoea. Accelerated transit; post-prandial, urgent, improves with fasting (hyperthyroidism, IBS).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Osmotic diarrhoea. Osmotically active substances (lactase deficiency, laxatives); stops with fasting.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Prolonged diarrhoea. 2 to 4 weeks; post-infectious or parasitic.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Secretory diarrhoea. Active secretion; persists during fasting (IBD, endocrine tumours, drugs).

title: Define diarrhoea and classify by duration.
subject: subj:semio

body.front: Define diarrhoea and classify by duration.
body.back: > 300 g/day, > 3/day, > 90% water. Acute < 2 weeks, prolonged 2-4 weeks, chronic > 4 weeks.
False diarrhoea (small hard stools < 300 g/day), anal incontinence, non-faecal discharge (blood, pus, mucus without stool).
Secretory (choleriform): toxin, profuse watery, dehydration, persists fasting. Invasive (dysenteric): bloody mucous stools, fever, pain, tenesmus.
Extreme ages, immunosuppression, comorbidities; dehydration (dry tongue, thirst, skin fold, hypotension, oliguria); dysenteric colitis, sepsis.

title: When are tests needed in acute diarrhoea?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: When are tests needed in acute diarrhoea?
body.back: Severe dehydration, blood or pus, fever > 38 °C, duration > 3 days, epidemic context or immunosuppression.
CBC, CRP, electrolytes, liver tests, protein electrophoresis, calcium, vitamin D, ferritin, albumin.
Malabsorptive, motor, osmotic, secretory, exudative.
Osmotic stops and motor improves with fasting; secretory and malabsorptive persist.
A clinical syndrome of diffuse abdominal pain, frequent stools with mucus, blood and/or pus, and false urges, reflecting the rectum's reaction to inflammatory, infectious or neoplastic disease.

Age, occupation, rural or urban setting; GI disease, immunosuppression (HIV, diabetes), tuberculosis, malignancy; surgery; antibiotics, immunosuppressants, chemo- or radiotherapy, antidiarrhoeals; travel; contacts, food and water; family history of colorectal cancer or IBD.

Severe cramps along the colon, focused on the left iliac fossa, with urgency; tenesmus (painful urge with empty rectum); false urges; non-faecal stools of mucus, pus and blood. Also fatigue, fever, weight loss, dehydration, vomiting, headache, myalgia, arthralgia.

title: What does the exam look for?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: What does the exam look for?
body.back: Dehydration (dry mucosa, poor turgor, sunken eyes); fever, tachycardia, hypotension (dehydration or sepsis), fast breathing; lower abdominal tenderness, guarding, hyperactive bowel sounds; rectal abscess, fistula, fissure, haemorrhoids, prolapse, mass, blood or mucus; joints, confusion, lymph nodes.

Blood count, CRP, electrolytes and renal function; HIV if recurrent; C. difficile toxin after antibiotics. Stool microscopy (RBC, WBC, mucus, Entamoeba) and culture (Shigella, Salmonella, Campylobacter, E. coli). Sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy with biopsy. CT if severe, atypical or complicated.
Colorectal cancer and polyps; IBD (ulcerative colitis, colonic Crohn's); infectious proctitis (Entamoeba histolytica, CMV, E. coli, Salmonella, Shigella); radiation colitis; ischaemic colitis.

Dysphagia: difficulty swallowing from mouth to stomach. Odynophagia: pain on swallowing. Aphagia: complete inability. Globus: lump sensation without real difficulty. Always clarify what the patient means.
Oropharyngeal (high): hard to start swallowing, cough, nasal regurgitation; neurological, muscular, ENT causes. Oesophageal (low): food sticking behind the sternum; mechanical or motor causes.

Organic (mechanical): lumen obstruction by tumour, stricture or foreign body; progressive, solids then liquids. Functional (motor): impaired peristalsis or sphincter relaxation (achalasia, spasm, scleroderma); intermittent, liquids too.

Age (elderly: rule out cancer); risk factors (alcohol, tobacco, caustics, GERD, radiotherapy); onset (sudden: foreign body; progressive: cancer or stricture; intermittent: motor); food type; associated symptoms (odynophagia: infection; heartburn: stricture; cough at meals: oropharyngeal; hoarseness: larynx; weight loss: cancer).
EGD first (mucosa, biopsy). Barium swallow for motility and Zenker's. Manometry for motor disorders. CT or EUS for staging or compression. Laryngoscopy for ENT causes.

Oesophageal: cancer (progressive, weight loss, smoking, alcohol), peptic stricture, achalasia, foreign body, benign tumour, caustic stenosis, infectious oesophagitis. Extrinsic: mediastinal tumours, aortic aneurysm, big left atrium. ENT: infection, cancers, Zenker's. Neurological: stroke, Parkinson's, ALS, MS, myasthenia, myopathies.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Upper GI endoscopy. First-line test: sees the mucosa and takes biopsies to exclude cancer.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Oropharyngeal dysphagia. Difficulty starting the swallow, cough, nasal regurgitation; neurological, muscular or ENT causes.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Oesophageal dysphagia. Food sticks behind the sternum; mechanical or motor disorders.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Motor dysphagia. Impaired peristalsis or LES relaxation: liquids as much as solids (paradoxical), intermittent.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Oesophageal phase. Involuntary peristalsis toward the stomach.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Oral phase. Voluntary transport of the bolus to the oropharynx.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Organic dysphagia. Obstruction (tumour, stricture): solids then liquids, constant and progressive.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Pharyngeal phase. Reflex closure of the larynx and propulsion into the oesophagus.

title: Define dysphagia, odynophagia, aphagia and globus.
subject: subj:semio

body.front: Define dysphagia, odynophagia, aphagia and globus.
body.back: Dysphagia: difficulty swallowing. Odynophagia: pain on swallowing. Aphagia: complete inability. Globus: lump sensation without true difficulty.
Oral (voluntary), pharyngeal (reflex laryngeal closure, propulsion), oesophageal (involuntary peristalsis).
Oropharyngeal: difficulty starting, cough, nasal regurgitation (neuro, muscle, ENT). Oesophageal: food sticking behind the sternum (mechanical or motor).

title: How does the type of food point to the mechanism?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: How does the type of food point to the mechanism?
body.back: Solids then liquids → organic obstruction. Liquids as much as or more than solids (paradoxical) → motor disorder such as achalasia.

title: Investigations for dysphagia and their roles?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: Investigations for dysphagia and their roles?
body.back: Endoscopy (first line, biopsy), barium swallow (motility, Zenker), manometry (peristalsis, LES), CT/EUS (staging, compression), laryngoscopy (ENT).
Solids and liquids from onset, paradoxical, intermittent, worse with hot or cold food, general state preserved; manometry: no peristalsis, non-relaxing LES.
Stroke, Parkinson's, ALS, multiple sclerosis, myasthenia gravis, myopathies.
Age > 50, rapidly progressive, weight loss > 5 kg, iron-deficiency anaemia, history of caustics, GERD or radiation.

title: Which digestive organs can be examined?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: Which digestive organs can be examined?
body.back: The mouth, the stomach, small intestine and colon, the anal region and lower rectum, and partly the liver and spleen.

title: How do you prepare for the exam?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: How do you prepare for the exam?
body.back: Check identity, explain and obtain consent, ensure an intimate, calm, warm room; patient lying flat, doctor on the patient's right.

title: What do you look for in the mouth?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: What do you look for in the mouth?
body.back: Teeth, gums, palate, cheeks, tongue, tonsils and uvula. Aphthous ulcers (IBD), atrophic glossitis (B12 deficiency), white plaques (candidiasis), angular cheilitis (iron deficiency).

title: What does the neck exam include?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: What does the neck exam include?
body.back: Cervical lymph nodes, especially the left supraclavicular node (digestive cancer metastasis), thyroid (moves with swallowing), vascular auscultation. The oesophagus cannot be examined directly.

title: What does abdominal inspection look for?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: What does abdominal inspection look for?
body.back: Surgical scars, hernia or eventration (hernia on a scar), collateral veins (portal hypertension), bulges or asymmetry, and skin lesions.
Supine, knees bent to relax the muscles; light then deep palpation of all quadrants with one or two hands, looking for masses, tenderness, pain, hepatomegaly and splenomegaly.

title: How are liver and spleen palpated?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: How are liver and spleen palpated?
body.back: Liver: under the right ribs, flat hand or hooked fingertips, with a deep breath that lowers the liver. Spleen: deep under the left ribs, hard to feel when normal; splenomegaly is easy and moves with breathing.

Percussion: tympany means air, dullness means dense organ or fluid; the abdomen is tympanic except over the liver and a full bladder. Auscultation: bowel sounds and arterial bruits, such as an aortic aneurysm.

title: How is the proctological exam done?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: How is the proctological exam done?
body.back: Explain and obtain consent in a private room; knee-chest or lateral (Sims) position; gloves and lubricant; inspect the anal skin, then digital exam of the anal canal, distal rectum and prostate.

GERD: reflux of gastric contents into the oesophagus causing symptoms and/or complications; chronic, relapsing. Physiological reflux: transient, postprandial, asymptomatic, no damage. Pathological: frequent or prolonged, with symptoms or lesions.

LES hypotonia, hiatal hernia (commonest anatomical cause), raised abdominal pressure (obesity, pregnancy, tight clothes), delayed gastric emptying, foods (fat, chocolate, caffeine, alcohol, mint, spice), drugs (nitrates, theophylline, anticholinergics, calcium blockers, progesterone, sedatives), smoking, late meals.

Pyrosis: retrosternal burning rising to the throat, postprandial or nocturnal, worse bending or lying, relieved by antacids. Regurgitation: effortless acid reflux into the mouth with a bitter taste. Also epigastric burning, belching, bloating, nausea, early satiety, water brash.

ENT and oral: dental erosions, gingivitis, pharyngitis, laryngitis, globus, hoarseness. Respiratory: nocturnal cough, asthma-like symptoms, recurrent bronchitis, laryngospasm. Chest: non-cardiac pseudo-anginal pain.

title: When are tests needed and which?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: When are tests needed and which?
body.back: For atypical or extra-digestive forms, alarm signs, poor response or age over 50. Endoscopy: oesophagitis, stricture, Barrett's; normal does not exclude GERD (NERD). pH-metry: pH under 4 over 5 percent of the time. Manometry, impedancemetry (non-acid reflux), barium swallow (stricture, hernia).
Peptic oesophagitis, bleeding (haematemesis, anaemia), peptic stricture (dysphagia), Barrett's oesophagus (cancer risk), respiratory complications (cough, asthma, aspiration).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Alarm signs. Dysphagia, odynophagia, bleeding, anaemia, weight loss, vomiting: endoscopy required.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Anti-reflux barrier. The lower oesophageal sphincter and diaphragmatic crura prevent reflux at rest.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Complications. Peptic oesophagitis, bleeding, peptic stricture, Barrett's oesophagus, respiratory complications.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Extra-digestive forms. ENT, respiratory and non-cardiac chest pain.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Predisposing factors. LES hypotonia, hiatal hernia, raised abdominal pressure, slow gastric emptying, foods and drugs.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: pH monitoring. Reference test: GERD confirmed if oesophageal pH is below 4 for more than 5% of the time.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Typical symptoms. Pyrosis (retrosternal burning rising to the throat) and regurgitation.
Physiological: transient, post-prandial, asymptomatic, no damage. Pathological: frequent or prolonged, causing symptoms, inflammation or complications.
LES hypotonia, hiatal hernia, raised abdominal pressure (obesity, pregnancy, tight clothing), delayed emptying, foods and drugs, smoking, alcohol, late meals.
Retrosternal burning rising from the epigastrium to the throat; post-prandial or nocturnal; worse bending or lying; relieved by antacids.
ENT/oral: dental erosions, pharyngitis, laryngitis, globus, hoarseness. Respiratory: nocturnal cough, asthma, bronchitis, laryngospasm. Non-cardiac chest pain.

title: When are tests needed in GERD?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: When are tests needed in GERD?
body.back: Atypical or extra-digestive forms, alarm signs, poor treatment response, age > 50, long-standing reflux.
Peptic oesophagitis (erosions, ulcers), peptic stricture, Barrett's oesophagus; normal in NERD.
24-h pH-metry (pH < 4 > 5% of time), manometry, impedance (non-acid reflux), barium swallow (stricture, hernia).
Enlargement of the whole liver or part of it. Diagnosis is clinical; the cause needs additional work-up.

Inspection for a right hypochondrial bulge; palpation of the anteroinferior border with deep inspiration and hooked fingers, plus percussion and auscultation. The upper limit by percussion from above; measure on the midclavicular line (normal under 12 cm). Left liver: palpation and percussion in the epigastrium.

title: How do you describe the liver?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: How do you describe the liver?
body.back: Normal: firm, regular border, smooth surface, painless. Abnormal: too soft or hard, sharp or irregular border, nodular surface, painful.
Left: masses of the stomach, transverse colon or pancreatic body. Right: liver ptosis, Riedel lobe, masses of the right colic flexure or right kidney, enlarged gallbladder.

Cirrhosis: firm to hard, irregular sharp border, nodular, painless. Cardiac: soft to firm, smooth, painful. Cholestasis or storage: firm or soft, smooth, painless. Neoplastic: hard, nodular, painful. Abscess: localised, smooth, intensely painful.

Tumours: benign (adenoma, cysts), malignant (metastasis, lymphoma, haemopathy, HCC). Metabolic: steatosis, Wilson's, haemochromatosis, Gaucher. Congestion: heart failure, Budd-Chiari. Inflammatory: HBV, HCV, sepsis, abscess, drugs, alcohol, granulomatosis, systemic disease. Cirrhosis, portal vein thrombosis.

HMG + splenomegaly + collaterals: cirrhosis with portal hypertension. HMG + right upper quadrant pain + fever: abscess. HMG + poor performance status + lower GI bleeding: colorectal cancer with metastases. Painful HMG + hepatojugular reflux: heart failure. HMG + neurological signs: Wilson's disease.
Excess bilirubin, typically above 35 µmol/L, causing yellow sclera and/or skin. A symptom of many diseases, needing a structured aetiological strategy based on bilirubin metabolism.
A pigment from haemoglobin breakdown, eliminated in bile, responsible for urine and stool colour.
Pruritus, dark urine, pale (acholic) stools, steatorrhoea, xanthoma and xanthelasma, and signs of fat-soluble vitamin (A, D, E, K) deficiency.

title: Give the lab findings of cholestasis.
subject: subj:semio

body.front: Give the lab findings of cholestasis.
body.back: Raised conjugated bilirubin, GGT, alkaline phosphatase, cholesterol and 5'-nucleotidase; prolonged prothrombin time (ratio under 70 percent).

Age, sex, occupation, chronic liver disease, liver or biliary surgery, autoimmune disease, viral hepatitis risk factors, travel, alcohol, smoking, drug use, medications and supplements, family history of jaundice or cancer.

title: What symptoms and signs do you look for?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: What symptoms and signs do you look for?
body.back: Onset and course of jaundice, cholestasis symptoms, fever, pain, dyspepsia, GI bleeding, diarrhoea, neurological signs, weight loss, joint pain; acute cholangitis = pain, fever, jaundice. Exam: GCS, asterixis, fetor hepaticus, oedema, sclera, scratch marks, purpura, spider angiomas, palmar erythema, gynaecomastia, tattoos, abdomen, rectum, nodes.

Blood count and smear, prothrombin time, liver function tests, protein electrophoresis, iron studies, haemolysis tests (LDH, haptoglobin, Coombs, Hb electrophoresis), autoimmune and viral serology, infection tests. Imaging: ultrasound, CT, MRI, endoscopic ultrasound, biopsy; ERCP is therapeutic.

First: cholestatic (conjugated) or not (unconjugated). Cholestatic: ultrasound for dilated ducts: yes = extrahepatic obstruction (e.g. biliary stones), no = intrahepatic (e.g. chronic liver disease). Non-cholestatic: think haemolysis, corpuscular (usually extravascular) or extracorpuscular (usually intravascular).

Nausea: unpleasant, subjective sensation often with the urge to vomit, from the GI tract or the CNS. Vomiting (emesis): forceful expulsion of stomach contents through the mouth, usually preceded by nausea; active mechanism of violent cyclic contractions of the abdominal muscles, diaphragm and respiratory muscles.

Stimuli (GI irritation, vestibular disturbances, higher cortical centres, CTZ stimulation by drugs or toxins) activate the vomiting centre, then the abdominal vagal afferents. The diaphragm and abdominal muscles contract strongly and the LES relaxes: forceful ejection of stomach contents through the mouth.

title: When is upper GI endoscopy indicated, and what can it find?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: When is upper GI endoscopy indicated, and what can it find?
body.back: Indications: suspected mucosal lesion, obstruction, complications (upper GI bleeding, oesophagitis, gastritis). It allows immediate biopsy. Findings: ulcers, erosions, masses, chronic GERD or Barrett's oesophagus; pictures show erosions, gastric ulcer, gastric cancer, pylorus obstruction.

title: What is the differential diagnosis of vomiting?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: What is the differential diagnosis of vomiting?
body.back: Gastro-oesophageal regurgitation: backward flow into the oesophagus without nausea. Rumination syndrome: repeated regurgitation of food into the mouth without nausea.

title: List the gastrointestinal causes of acute vomiting.
subject: subj:semio

body.front: List the gastrointestinal causes of acute vomiting.
body.back: Gastroenteritis (viral, bacterial, parasitic), food poisoning. Surgical abdomen: peritonitis, appendicitis, cholecystitis, intestinal obstruction. Non-surgical: acute pancreatitis, biliary colic, peptic ulcer, acute gastritis (often NSAIDs).

title: List the non-digestive causes of acute vomiting.
subject: subj:semio

body.front: List the non-digestive causes of acute vomiting.
body.back: Metabolic/endocrine: DKA, adrenal crisis, hyperthyroidism, hypercalcaemia. Neurological: raised ICP (head injury, stroke, tumour), meningitis, migraine, vestibular disorders. Cardiovascular: MI, aortic dissection. Infectious: sepsis, pyelonephritis. Pregnancy: hyperemesis gravidarum. Electrolytes: hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia. Toxic: chemotherapy, antibiotics, opioids, alcohol, heavy metals. Psychogenic: anxiety, bulimia.

title: List the causes of chronic vomiting.
subject: subj:semio

body.front: List the causes of chronic vomiting.
body.back: GI: pyloroduodenal stenosis, GERD, gastroparesis (diabetes), chronic pancreatitis, IBS, chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction, coeliac disease, gastric cancer. Non-GI: chronic renal failure (uraemia), hyperthyroidism, Addison's; chronic migraine, intracranial tumours, chronic raised ICP; long-term NSAIDs, opioids, antibiotics, chronic alcohol; functional, binge-purge, psychogenic vomiting.

title: What are the complications of vomiting?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: What are the complications of vomiting?
body.back: Hydro-electrolytic: dehydration, hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia, metabolic alkalosis. Mechanical: Mallory-Weiss (mucosal tear at the gastro-oesophageal junction, bleeding); Boerhaave (life-threatening oesophageal rupture, leakage into the mediastinum). Infectious: aspiration pneumonia (fever, cough, dyspnoea).

title: What do you ask in the history?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: What do you ask in the history?
body.back: Age; medical and surgical history, especially digestive; medications (type, dose, date of last intake); toxic exposure; recent travel; similar cases in family or close contacts; last menstrual period and contraception.

title: Which characteristics of vomiting do you describe?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: Which characteristics of vomiting do you describe?
body.back: Onset and duration (acute, chronic, recurrent), circumstances (spontaneous or induced), frequency, content, volume, triggers and relieving factors (diet, head position), pattern and timing, impact (appetite, hydration, weight, general condition).

title: What does the timing of vomiting suggest?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: What does the timing of vomiting suggest?
body.back: Morning: pregnancy or alcohol dependence. Early postprandial: gastric emptying disorder or gastroparesis. Late postprandial: duodenal or pyloric obstruction. During meals: psychogenic cause.

title: What does the content of vomit suggest?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: What does the content of vomit suggest?
body.back: Clear fluid: acid reflux or regurgitation. Undigested food: gastroparesis or gastric outlet obstruction. Bile: bile reflux. Blood (haematemesis): active upper GI bleeding. Feculent: severe bowel obstruction.
Nausea, abdominal pain, diarrhoea, myalgias, fever; extra-digestive: headache, photophobia (meningeal syndrome), altered consciousness.

General: dehydration (dry mucosae, reduced skin turgor, sunken eyes), vital signs, temperature. Abdomen: distension, scars, tenderness, masses, bowel sounds (hyperactive: obstruction; absent: ileus), percussion for ascites or mass. Neurological: headache, papilledema (raised ICP); altered mental status, dizziness, nystagmus (CNS). Cardiovascular: heart failure. Lymph nodes: infection or malignancy.

Persistent vomiting or inability to keep oral intake; severe or progressive abdominal pain; haematemesis; fever; neurological symptoms (severe headache, altered consciousness); dehydration; unintentional weight loss; bilious or feculent vomiting (obstruction); elderly patient; immunocompromised state.

title: Which initial tests do you order?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: Which initial tests do you order?
body.back: CBC; electrolytes (Na, K, Cl, HCO3); renal function; glucose (DKA); hCG in women of reproductive age; thyroid tests if hyperthyroidism is suspected; urinalysis for ketones. Then as indicated: upper GI endoscopy, ultrasound, CT, ECG (hypokalaemia), cerebral CT, endocrine or toxicological tests.

title: Give the four steps of the chest exam.
subject: subj:semio

body.front: Give the four steps of the chest exam.
body.back: After the interview: inspection, palpation, percussion and auscultation; the signs are grouped into syndromes, then further tests lead to the diagnosis.
Naked chest, patient seated or standing, in full light, watching the patient undress for dyspnoea, inspecting the whole thorax. Note general appearance: pallor, cyanosis, dyspnoea, thinness, oedema.

title: How is percussion done, and what does it show?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: How is percussion done, and what does it show?
body.back: The middle finger of the dominant hand strikes the distal joint of the other hand's middle finger on an intercostal space, comparing both sides at each level. Normal lung is resonant; liver and heart dull. Dull: pleurisy, pachypleuritis, consolidation. Hyperresonant: pneumothorax, emphysema.
Vesicular: parenchymal noise over both lungs, mainly inspiration and early expiration. Bronchial: loud, high-pitched, over the sternum. Tracheal: very loud, over the neck, in both phases.

title: When are breath sounds reduced or absent?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: When are breath sounds reduced or absent?
body.back: Generalised: upper airway obstruction, advanced emphysema, severe asthma. Localised to one side: pleural effusion, pneumothorax, hydropneumothorax, main bronchus obstruction, tumour, pneumonia or collapse.

Wheeze: whistling from narrowed airways. Rhonchi: low-pitched snoring. Crackles: coarse (rice krispies: fluid, infection) or fine (velcro: fluid, infection, fibrosis). Rub: end-inspiratory, foot in fresh snow. Stridor: loud inspiratory monophonic wheeze of upper airway obstruction.

Consolidation: dull, bronchial breathing, coarse crackles, increased vocal resonance. Effusion: dull, absent breath sounds, possible rub, decreased resonance. Pneumothorax: hyperresonant, absent sounds, decreased resonance. Fibrosis and pulmonary oedema: normal percussion, fine crackles.

title: What does the general exam add?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: What does the general exam add?
body.back: Cardiovascular: right heart failure, pericarditis (report in pleurisy). Abdominal: ascites, hepato- or splenomegaly (report in pleurisy). ENT infection. Lymph nodes (tuberculosis, lymphoma, sarcoidosis). Urogenital and pelvic. Neurological: meningeal signs in tuberculosis, pleurisy or miliary.

Barrel chest: bilateral distension (emphysema, asthma). Unilateral distension: pleurisy, parietal tumour. Retraction: unilateral, or whole (pachypleuritis). Deformities: pectus excavatum, carinatum, arcuatum. Spine: kyphosis, lordosis, scoliosis.
Adults 12 to 20/min; infants and neonates 30 to 60/min. Polypnoea over 20; bradypnoea under 12. Also note inspiration and expiration duration, stridor or wheeze, and expansion.

title: List the signs of increased work of breathing.
subject: subj:semio

body.front: List the signs of increased work of breathing.
body.back: Tripod position; accessory muscle use (sternocleidomastoid, scalenes); nasal flaring; intercostal, subcostal, suprasternal and supraclavicular retractions; grunting; pursed lips; expiratory abdominal contraction; paradoxical thoracoabdominal breathing.

Malar redness, Horner signs, herpes, scars, tattoos, oedema, jugular venous distension, collateral circulation, cyanosis, eczema, erythema nodosum, joint deformities, superior vena cava swelling of face and arms, wall masses.

title: Describe digital clubbing and its tests.
subject: subj:semio

body.front: Describe digital clubbing and its tests.
body.back: Nails enlarged and curved (Hippocratic), with swollen distal phalanges: chronic hypoxaemia. Lovibond angle of 180 degrees or more. Schamroth test: the diamond window between opposed nails disappears.

title: What is Pierre Marie hypertrophic osteoarthropathy?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: What is Pierre Marie hypertrophic osteoarthropathy?
body.back: A hereditary or paraneoplastic syndrome: painful clubbing, hypertrophy of extremities with synovial effusions, vasomotor disorders, arthralgia, and radiological periostitis of long bones.
Disruption of the sympathetic pathway to one side of the face: miosis, ptosis with apparent enophthalmos, and anhidrosis.

title: How is palpation done, and what does fremitus show?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: How is palpation done, and what does fremitus show?
body.back: Warm hands, seated patient, bilateral and symmetrical; the patient says toy boat (44 in Arabic, 33 in French). Fremitus is increased in pneumonia; decreased or abolished in pleurisy, pneumothorax, atelectasis and emphysema bullae. Palpation also finds painful points, subcutaneous emphysema, masses, nodes and expansion.

A rapid, short, deep inspiration with an open glottis, followed by a sudden, explosive, noisy expiration. It keeps the airways open by clearing secretions and particles. Non-specific, it accompanies almost any respiratory disease.

An involuntary but controllable defence reflex. A productive cough should be respected; a useless dry irritative cough should be treated. Triggers: mechanical (smoke, dust, mucus), chemical (gastric acid in GERD) and thermal (cold air).

Sudden coughing up of an abundant purulent collection, often with nausea; massive over 100 mL, fractionated or nummular. Clear: hydatid cyst. Pus: abscess. Pus and bile: liver abscess with bronchial fistula. Chocolate: amoebic abscess.
Hemoptysis: respiratory history, coughing, bright red, aerated, frothy blood. Haematemesis: digestive history, vomiting, dark non-aerated venous blood, sometimes with food.

Low under 50 mL; medium 300 to 500 mL; high over 500 mL at once or in 24 h. Same significance whatever the amount: an emergency. Severe: shock and respiratory distress. Moderate: malaise, laryngeal tingling, metallic taste, stable haemodynamics. Blood count falls.

Bronchopulmonary: cancer, tuberculosis, bronchiectasis, ruptured hydatid cyst, pneumonia, foreign body. Cardiovascular: valvulopathy, pulmonary oedema, embolism. Others: trauma, bleeding disorders. Idiopathic in 15 percent.

Onset (sudden stabbing: pneumothorax; progressive: cancer), intensity, location and radiation, triggers (cough, position, breathing, palpation), associated signs, course, analgesic position and type (acute, chronic, phrenic neuralgia along the sternal edges).

title: Give the acute causes of chest pain.
subject: subj:semio

body.front: Give the acute causes of chest pain.
body.back: Acute coronary syndrome (retrosternal oppression radiating to arms or jaw), pulmonary embolism, aortic dissection (radiating to the back), oesophageal rupture (after vomiting), pneumothorax, pneumonia, pericarditis (relieved leaning forward), pleurisy, digestive and parietal causes, psychogenic (after excluding organic causes).

title: Give the chronic causes of chest pain.
subject: subj:semio

body.front: Give the chronic causes of chest pain.
body.back: Cardiovascular: hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, tight aortic stenosis, pulmonary hypertension. Pleural: chronic pleurisy, mesothelioma. Mediastinal tumours. Digestive: GERD, pancreatitis, pancreatic or oesophageal cancer, gallstones (right shoulder). Parenchymal and parietal: cancer, metastases, spondylodiscitis.

title: Describe the mechanism and analysis of dyspnoea.
subject: subj:semio

body.front: Describe the mechanism and analysis of dyspnoea.
body.back: Breathing discomfort; normal rate about 16/min. It can come from any step: central control, the thoracic cage, airways, parenchyma, gas exchange or transport. Analyse onset (acute or chronic), intensity (NYHA, mMRC), type, timing, triggers and associated symptoms.

Inspiratory: high obstruction. Expiratory: low obstruction (asthma). Orthopnoea: lying flat. Platypnoea: on sitting up. Apnoea, polypnoea, bradypnoea by rate. Paroxysmal nocturnal: heart failure. Postprandial: GERD, aspiration, food allergy.

Acute: laryngotracheal (spasm, oedema, foreign body), bronchial (asthma), pulmonary (pneumonia, miliary), pleural (pleurisy, pneumothorax), cardiovascular (embolism, heart failure, pulmonary oedema). Chronic: COPD, asthma, bronchiectasis, tuberculosis, sarcoidosis, chronic pleurisy, recurrent embolism, left heart disease, mediastinal compression.

External ear canal, posterior pharynx, retrotonsillar space, inter-arytenoid larynx, trachea, carina and large bronchi (spurs especially), plus pleura, mediastinum, pericardium, diaphragm, oesophagus, stomach, and even the gallbladder, appendix and utero-adnexal regions.

title: Classify cough by duration and type.
subject: subj:semio

body.front: Classify cough by duration and type.
body.back: Acute under 3 weeks, subacute 3 to 8 weeks, chronic over 8 weeks. Dry or productive. Permanent (sinus infection, cancer, whooping cough, fibrosis) or intermittent (allergy, GERD, bronchial hyperreactivity).

title: Link cough timing and triggers to causes.
subject: subj:semio

body.front: Link cough timing and triggers to causes.
body.back: Nocturnal: GERD, asthma. Morning: bronchiectasis, chronic bronchitis. Postprandial: GERD. Position change: pleurisy, GERD. Supine: GERD, left heart failure. Exercise: asthma, heart failure. Cold, humidity, laughter, odours: asthma.
Bitonal: recurrent nerve compression or paralysis. Painful: pleural or parietal involvement. Emetogenic (with vomiting): especially in children.

title: List the causes of chronic cough.
subject: subj:semio

body.front: List the causes of chronic cough.
body.back: Productive: chronic bronchitis, bronchiectasis, tuberculosis, bronchial cancer, asthma. Dry: bronchial cancer, interstitial lung disease, asthma, rhinitis or rhinosinusitis, GERD, ACE inhibitors, psychogenic.

Sputum: abnormal secretions from the subglottic airways coughed into the mouth. Excessive expectoration: over 30 mL/day. Bronchorrhoea: over 100 mL/day. Women and children often swallow sputum. Distinguish from nasal discharge.

Mucus traps inhaled particles and pathogens and coordinated cilia push it upward and out, protecting the lung. Irritation increases mucus, cleared by coughing. Clearance is reduced in bronchiectasis, chronic bronchitis, cystic fibrosis, primary ciliary dyskinesia and Kartagener syndrome, and in smokers.

Serous (transparent), mucous (colourless with grey gummy masses), purulent (frank pus), mucopurulent, frothy (white, aerated, sometimes pink), pearly (asthma, Laennec), haemoptoic (same value as hemoptysis).

title: Describe the pleural fluid effusion syndrome.
subject: subj:semio

body.front: Describe the pleural fluid effusion syndrome.
body.back: Fluid in the pleural cavity. Progressive onset with chest pain, dry cough and dyspnoea; fever depending on cause. Exam: reduced or abolished fremitus, dullness, reduced or absent breath sounds, sometimes a pleural rub. Complete general exam.

title: What does the X-ray show in an effusion?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: What does the X-ray show in an effusion?
body.back: Homogeneous opacity with a meniscus-shaped margin and blunting of the costophrenic angle. Small: blunted sulcus only. Large: whole hemithorax opaque, mediastinal shift and tracheal deviation away.

Damaged alveoli distend into large air spaces; centrilobular (blue bloater) or panlobular (pink puffer). Cough, worsening dyspnoea, barrel chest, polypnoea, diffuse hyperresonance, decreased fremitus and breath sounds. X-ray: increased AP diameter and retrosternal space.

Loss of lung substance from a tuberculous cavern, lung abscess, excavated cancer or ruptured hydatid cyst. Fever, cough, expectoration, vomica; dullness, increased fremitus, subcrackles; an excavated image on X-ray.

Acute bronchitis: mucosal inflammation, dry then productive cough, often normal exam and X-ray. Chronic bronchitis: cough and sputum 3 months a year for 2 years; barrel chest, clubbing, cyanosis. Bronchiectasis: permanent dilatation of 3rd to 8th order bronchi, morning bronchorrhoea, clubbing, rhonchi; CT and bronchoscopy.
Clinical and radiological signs from irritation or compression of mediastinal organs: respiratory (dyspnoea, dry cough, rare hemoptysis), circulatory, neurological and digestive.

Obstruction of SVC flow, mostly thrombus or tumour. Early: dizziness, tinnitus, headache, eyelid oedema, jugular turgor. Late: oedema of face, neck and thorax, collateral veins, telangiectasia, cyanosis worse on coughing. Without an opacity, think SVC thrombosis (Behçet) or fibrous mediastinitis. IVC syndrome (rarer): hepatomegaly, ascites, leg oedema.

title: Name the neurological and digestive mediastinal signs.
subject: subj:semio

body.front: Name the neurological and digestive mediastinal signs.
body.back: Sympathetic: Horner syndrome; with apex tumour and bone lysis, Pancoast-Tobias syndrome. Phrenic: hiccups, girdle neuralgia, diaphragmatic paralysis. Recurrent: dysphonia or aphonia. Vagus: dyspnoea, bradycardia, sialorrhoea. Oesophageal compression: dysphagia, posterior opacity (neurinoma).

Sitting, with or without local anaesthesia, in the zone of complete dullness, shaving the upper edge of the lower rib. It confirms the effusion, shows its gross appearance (serofibrinous, purulent, haemorrhagic, chyliform) and provides samples.
Exudate: albumin over 30 g/L, inflammatory origin. Transudate: albumin under 30 g/L, mechanical origin. Pleural biopsy and thoracoscopy confirm the cause.

Air in the pleural cavity collapsing the lung. Spontaneous, traumatic or iatrogenic; primary (no lesion) or secondary (pre-existing disease). Air comes through a visceral pleural breach (ruptured emphysema bleb) or a parietal breach (chest wound).

title: What are the clinical signs of pneumothorax?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: What are the clinical signs of pneumothorax?
body.back: Sudden stabbing sub-mammary or subscapular pain, dyspnoea and dry cough. The hemithorax is distended and painful with reduced expansion, decreased fremitus, hyperresonance and reduced or absent breath sounds.

title: What does imaging show in pneumothorax?
subject: subj:semio

body.front: What does imaging show in pneumothorax?
body.back: A hyperlucent area devoid of bronchovascular markings, bounded by a thin visceral pleural line around the collapsed lung. Effects on neighbours: contralateral mediastinal shift, depressed hemidiaphragm, widened intercostal spaces. Treated by needle aspiration.

Air and fluid together: pneumothorax symptoms, with fluid signs at the base topped by air signs; on X-ray an opacity surmounted by lucency. Fluid: yellow (hydro-), pus (pyo-), blood (haemo-) or chyle (chylo-pneumothorax).

A lobe or segment no longer ventilates, often filled with alveolar exudate. Increased fremitus, dullness, bronchial breath sounds, crackles. X-ray: dense homogeneous confluent opacity with indistinct borders, air bronchogram, systematised to a lobe or segment.

Non-retracted: acute pneumonia, pulmonary infarction, tuberculous pneumonia. Retracted: intrinsic or extrinsic bronchial stenosis, parenchymal destruction; structures shift toward the affected side with rib crowding.
